There's a New Motorcycle Race Engine in Town, Triumph's Moto2 Triple Lands in 2027
38 photos
Photo: Triumph
After back in the scorching days of August, British bike maker Triumph let slip the first details on the new engine that will be used in the MotoGP Moto2 World Championship, it came back on the matter this week and fully revealed the changes it made. And let me tell you, there is plenty to talk about.
Triumph has been the sole engine supplier for Moto2 ever since 2019, and it has constantly improved the makeup and capabilities of the 765cc triple that was used in the bikes raced by young riders. What happens for the upcoming season, though, marks the biggest change made to it over the past seven years.
First up, the engine is now larger, having grown from 765cc to 798cc. This was achieved, among other things, by means of deploying a new crankshaft and a 2.25 mm longer stroke – the bore, however, stays put at 78 mm.
The Brits say they have completely redesigned the cylinder head, fitting it with a finger-follower valvetrain and titanium inlet valves. The inlet and exhaust valves are larger than they used to be, the intake ports have been redesigned, and there's a new, twin airbox that allows an increase of ten percent in airflow and more aggressive cam profiles.
Photo: Triumph Finally, Triumph's engineers installed new high-flow Bosch fuel injectors to improve fuel delivery and burn, and reimagined the combustion chamber that, together with the new pistons, increases the compression ratio from 13.5:1 to 14.0:1.
The engine also comes along with increased power levels (by that I mean both hp and torque) – not insanely larger, but still large enough to make a difference on the tracks, in the heat of the race, for talented riders.
In its current form, the Triumph Moto2 powerplant is rated at 128 horsepower, but the new 2027 unit takes that higher by some six percent – that would translate to a max horsepower level of 136 hp.
When it comes to torque, Triumph worked its magic and now says that the engine delivers more of it throughout the rev range - speaking of that, the powerplant's max rev sits at an impressive 13,800 rpm.
Photo: Triumph To accommodate the changes made to the powerplant, Triumph also had to make some upgrades to the things that tie into it, including the primary drive and the transmission. Sadly, we're not told exactly what those changes are.
Finally, there is also talk of the engine as a whole dropping some of its weight, thanks to the lighter cylinder head, for instance – the larger-displacement powerplant tips the scales almost five pounds (2.2 pounds) faster than the one it replaces.
We're told the upgrades mentioned above have not been implemented on a whim, but as a result of data gathered over some 1.2 million miles (two million km) of travel from riders that climbed not only on the back of the Moto2 race bikes, but also the other two-wheelers that carry this kind of powerplant in their frames, like the Street Triple 765 RS.
Triumph is now getting ready to start official testing of the powerplant ahead of the 2027 Moto2 season opener in March. In some way, though, that has been happening for a while now, as the new engine will require new chassis to support it, on account of the changes made to the air intake position and engine mounting points. According to the Brits, manufacturers have been testing solutions to those upgrades for about a year now.
Photo: Triumph The engine Triumph has been supplying Moto2 rides with has more than proven its worth on the track, even if, technically speaking, it is only competing against itself. We're told that in the eight years or so it has been raced, the triple has been responsible for setting no less than 89 all-time records and 77 race records. Of that, no less than 37 were achieved in 2025.
To mark the launch of the new Moto2 race engine, which is expected not only to follow in the footsteps of its predecessor, but also surpass it, Triumph released on the same day the details of the powerplant of a motorcycle that's meant to honor it. They call it Street Triple 798 Moto2 Edition , and it builds on the previously unveiled Street Triple 798 RS.
Packing the same displacement engine that'll go into the Moto2 racers, the bike is one of the lightest around, tipping the scales at 399 pounds (181 kg, wet weight). There will only be 1,000 units of this motorcycle made, evenly divided into two body colors, and each of them sells for $17,295. These bikes should be on the roads by May 2027.
We will keep an eye on what comes next for the new race engine and report back when something new comes along. In the meantime, you can enjoy the way it looks in the attached gallery, where it's shown both on its own and installed in the frame of the Moto2 Edition.
